title: We put 46 viewer complaints about *Ode to Joy* to screenwriter Yuan Zidan. She answered every one
excerpt: "I've always felt viewers misunderstand one thing. They ask us why these women have it so easy. Does having money and status mean you have it easy?"
body:
"I've always felt viewers misunderstand one thing. They ask us why these women have it so easy. Does having money and status mean you have it easy?"

Before *Ode to Joy* went on the air, the broadcasters — Dragon Television, Zhejiang Television and several big video sites — all sold the urban drama with the same tag: "another show from Hou Hongliang's team, after *Nirvana in Fire* and *The Disguiser*."

Remember that *Nirvana in Fire* and *The Disguiser* were the two most admired television dramas of the previous year. The creative team behind them, producer Hou Hongliang and director Kong Sheng included, was pushed into the spotlight, and people realized that this team — which had made *Parents' Love*, *Trek to the Northeast* and *A Family from Wenzhou* — was moving away from traditional military and business dramas toward material for younger viewers.

*Ode to Joy* was Hou Hongliang and company's new attempt to build a contemporary-drama brand. Also adapted from an online novel, it was more or less an "urban women's drama," unlike every "serious drama" they had made before. The team also tried full-scale marketing across Weibo, WeChat and Facebook, dropping its old "orthodox" face.

It worked. People had misgivings about a team of "straight men" making a women's drama, yet audiences turned out in force. From its premiere in April 2016 to the finale on May 10, [*Ode to Joy* drew 11 billion online views, past the 10 billion *The Legend of Miyue* had reached when it ended last year, and its national television rating hit 2.143](http://news.163.com/16/0512/07/BMRLR4N600014AED.html). [Hou Hongliang told the *Beijing Youth Daily*](http://news.xinhuanet.com/fashion/2016-05/11/c_128975173.htm) that he had not expected *Ode to Joy* to take off so fast — it spread in a couple of days, faster even than *Nirvana in Fire*.

What came next was less expected. Unlike *Nirvana in Fire*, the talk around *Ode to Joy* was full of criticism. Its Douban score slid to 7.3, far below the 9.2 for *Nirvana in Fire*, which Kong Sheng also directed. Some people questioned the show's values, arguing that this contemporary urban drama about five young women was an ode to money, not an ode to joy.

From the start, *Ode to Joy* was planned as a multi-season show: the same cast, supporting actors included, across three seasons. But soon after season one began airing, viewers were saying the "plot drags" and the "characters fall apart." It tried to borrow the multi-thread storytelling of American television, and something always felt off. The actors who had only just won real popularity were dragged down by it to varying degrees — "embarrassing," people said.

We wanted to know how a reputation turns that fast, so we gathered 46 of the most frequently repeated complaints on social media and put them to *Ode to Joy* screenwriter Yuan Zidan. She answered all of them.

**Q: QDaily**

**Y: Yuan Zidan, screenwriter of *Ode to Joy***

**Q: Some viewers feel the characters aren't treated fairly — that the flaws of Andy and Qu Xiaoxiao, the two rich ones, get prettied up, while the other three don't get the same treatment.**

Y: I find the whole notion of "prettying up" strange. It's precisely because we showed so many of Qu Xiaoxiao's flaws that so many people dislike her. Andy comes off as more perfect by comparison, because she's close to the woman we imagine as ideal. But she has her own troubles — she doesn't want to get close to anyone, for reasons rooted in her past, and that's a kind of urban illness too.

People say we dote on one character and try to cover for her. We don't. I think the reason people feel wronged on behalf of the other three girls is that the other two aren't that good either. It's exactly because we showed their flaws that people are asking the question.

Andy is smarter, Qu Xiaoxiao is richer — does that prove we like them better? Not necessarily. I've always felt viewers misunderstand one thing. They ask us why these two have it so easy. Does having money and status mean you have it easy?

Andy takes a heavy blow from what she learns about her family. Qu Xiaoxiao loses the man she loves, is looked down on by him, and her home life is far from harmonious. In some ways she's less happy and less whole than Little Earthworm. Or take Guanguan: her parents love her so much, and she's full of hope. What counts as happiness, what counts as having it easy, what counts as success — change your vantage point and you get a different answer.

All five girls have flaws. We've never shied away from that.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702141641xEGWLsP1opm4iCVA.jpg-w600)

**Q: Was Qu Xiaoxiao's screaming in the script?**

Y: It was. It's in the novel, it's in the script, and of course the actress screamed too. Ha ha ha ha.

**Q: "Qu Xiaoxiao should have been written as a mute. World peace."**

Y: That one doesn't need an answer. It's just venting.

**Q: Some people think "the screenwriter is writing herself into Qu Xiaoxiao, and Andy and the flatmates all praise her and look up to her."**

Y: Not at all. Plenty of people in the show criticize her. The three women in 2203 are all wary of her and would rather not go to her with a problem. When Little Guan's suitor came looking for her, he badly didn't want Qu Xiaoxiao to see. Little Earthworm has gone head to head with her several times. Andy disagrees with her views. And with Sister Fan — we shouldn't be so quick to throw stones at people.

I think to some degree people are choosing not to see this. We're not deliberately praising one person and criticizing another. We want to give viewers different angles for thinking about things, not just one. There's a line in the show: you shouldn't box someone in — mistress, gold-digger — those labels are what shape how you see her.

If Qu Xiaoxiao weren't a rich kid, people wouldn't find her behavior nearly as off-putting. It's like Sister Fan: once you've seen her family, you understand why she is the way she is. Qu Xiaoxiao's character has its causes too.

Each of the girls maps onto certain flaws. If watching the show makes people feel those flaws are bad, then fix them if you have them, and take it as a spur to do better if you don't.

**Q: "Miss Qu doesn't count as a rich kid — she acts exactly like some new-money upstart from a one-street town. Her attempts at being clever misfire and she turns into a ruffled-up feather duster, swatting at everything in reach."**

Y: There's no single mold for rich kids. They're a whole population, not one person. There's no rule that says they should be arrogant, or that they shouldn't. That's just a preconceived idea. They're all sorts of people; Qu Xiaoxiao happens to be this sort. And it fits her family: her parents built their money from nothing, she never studied much and she has no depth. That comes out of where she's from and who she is.

And the idea that rich kids ought to be gentle, modest and deferential — I really can't agree with that. I'm sure everyone has met plenty of impressive rich kids in life, plenty of unimpressive ones, and plenty who, like Qu Xiaoxiao, are impressive and unimpressive at once. I'd still rather people didn't slap labels on them.

**Q: "Qu Xiaoxiao makes one casual phone call and lands a whole project — isn't the work and business material far too childish?"**

Y: Yes, that's one of season one's problems. The novel doesn't have much on that side of things. At the time we discussed bringing in professional consultants, through the original author, to handle that part. But season one doesn't involve much business, so we never got around to finding them.

All we can say is that we tried. Now that the show has aired, viewers who know that world are telling us what's wrong, and we'll work to do better next season.

We thought more about drama than about professional accuracy.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702141642rlc4qXfnLPKT1oSa.jpg-w600)

**Q: "Would someone as independent as Andy really like Qu Xiaoxiao?"**

Y: Hard to say. Andy is a special case in the show. She has trouble with social interaction and finds it genuinely hard to build close relationships. So whether it's her relationship with Qidian or her dealings with the people on the 22nd floor, she's a passive personality. In a sense she's the one being won over.

Because she has little experience with people, someone as forward as Qu Xiaoxiao finds it easier to become her friend. Within the show, I think that holds up.

I'm sure that without the 22nd floor they'd have no overlap at all. With the 22nd floor, the overlap forms on its own.

**Q: One theory going around is that "the author approves of Qu most, and she gets the best ending." Is that right?**

Y: No. First, I can't speak for the author, because I didn't write the book. Whether the novel likes Little Qu best, I can't say.

From reading the novel myself and writing the script, I don't think it does. As I said, whether she has the smoothest ride depends on how you look at it. If your standard is making the most money and living the loudest, then sure, you might think Qu Xiaoxiao is the happiest. But I don't think the happiness Qiu Yingying gets from selling one bag of coffee is any smaller than the happiness Andy gets from closing a deal.

I think the two are worth the same. The distance between them can't be avoided; in ordinary life, differences between two people are inevitable. Let's not call it a gap, let's call it a difference. But when it comes to pursuing your own happiness and wholeness, there's no ranking.

People favor Little Qu precisely because she has more resources, but resources aren't success, and they aren't happiness. People have noticed it themselves: around episode ten they like one character and dislike another, and by episode twenty it's reversed. So all five of these girls have a lot of room to develop.

As for the guessing — first, the book isn't the show. The show will develop differently, and there's no need to force the book's characters onto the show's.

Second, I still think values aren't measured in material terms alone. Little Qu will hit setbacks too, just not the ones people imagine. Rather than everyone adoring her, she's a character who rises first and falls later.

And in terms of who gains the most happiness, security or growth, I don't think it's her.

Across the whole show — we're doing three seasons — Fan Shengmei is the character who grows the most inwardly. And if you're asking who is most worth learning from, it's unquestionably Little Earthworm. Nobody else compares. She's the one who considers herself the happiest.

**Q: "I don't get how Andy can calmly send a WeChat message about the neighbors fighting next door, something about the smell of everyday life. Andy's god's-eye attitude — oh, look at their messy little lives — plus the blank acting make her seem like an artificial-intelligence doll."**

Y: First, Andy judged whether stepping in was necessary, and at that point the situation didn't call for it. Second, as I said, people are messy and they gossip, and I think that scene is exactly what makes Andy feel human.

People should understand one thing: however close a friendship is, she has no obligation. Friends aren't there to do everything for you and solve every problem. They have no such obligation.

Also, the friendships on the 22nd floor build gradually. At first Andy didn't think much of Little Qiu — the line "don't argue with a fool" was originally about her. But little by little she saw that Little Qiu's courage and warmth were worth admiring, and only then did they become friends.

**Q: "Liu Tao's lead-character halo is obvious, and the lead's backstory is a cliché."**

Y: Is it a cliché? It doesn't feel like there are many leads like her. Every lead has some halo; it stands for a more idealized kind of woman. And if we spent dozens of episodes on a completely ordinary woman, maybe nobody would watch.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702141642Qdv7NeI9gZ8ta4lP.jpg-w600)

**Q: "Don't tell me Yang Zi's character is so dumb that people want a Qiu Yingying-free cut because Yang Zi acts well. This character has nothing to do with acting, right?"**

Y: I think it is Yang Zi's acting. She gave this naive sweetheart real character, and she really did show that playing a naive sweetheart can display acting ability.

First, now that people have seen the whole show, their view of Qiu Yingying has changed a great deal. Second, watching is easy, because you have the all-knowing god's-eye view. For Qiu Yingying, this is the life she's living; it is absolutely not a television drama seen from above.

I've met so many girls like this in my own life. Qiu Yingying agonized for one month and then pulled herself together and went looking for work. In real life I've seen no shortage of people who, after a breakup, mutter away like Xianglin's Wife and can't get free of it for six months or a year.

So I don't think people need to judge the characters so harshly. People dislike Qiu Yingying because they see themselves in her — they've lived through that same helpless stretch and discovered how much they dislike themselves. Yang Zi played it so well that she reminds people of their own bedraggled selves and of friends who irritated them. Honestly, most girls like this mean no harm. They're just naive and love too hard.

**Q: Some people say the show gives us "a naive sweetheart run in circles by a scumbag who finally loses her job; a good girl who refuses to settle, chases Prince Charming, and pines after a doctor who already has a girlfriend; a gold-digger who passes over a reliable classmate and throws herself at a man to support her family; a rich kid with nothing in common with the doctor who insists on clinging to him; and a high-flying executive who ignores two considerate men and goes for the troublemaker instead." How did you think about this cast structure?**

Y: What do you mean "already has a girlfriend" — why shouldn't the man she pines after have a girlfriend? The logic doesn't hold. These things aren't cause and effect. This is the kind of question that shouldn't be answered, because the thinking behind it is muddled.

**Q: Is there a gap between the five characters on the page and the five the actors played?**

Y: On the whole the gap isn't large, because the performances stayed faithful to both the novel and the script. But of course the actors added personal touches to make each one stand out more.

With five girls especially, each actor drew her own distinctions. Some performances are more exaggerated; Qu Xiaoxiao's is. People say Fan Shengmei's acting is explosive, and that's really because the novel and the script gave her the most room. Little Earthworm was played very endearingly. Guanguan had less written for her, so there was less room to perform. Andy is a more masculine role — logical, particular about clothes — and Sister Tao was very careful about that too. I'd say they all did the job excellently, close to what we imagined.

**Q: Why did Fan Shengmei's character get so much room?**

Y: Because season one has only three main storylines. One is the Manager Bai business, which runs for a stretch. The season's two big lines and two big mysteries are Fan Shengmei's family troubles and Andy's parentage. So those two get relatively more screen time. We made a small split between the older group and the younger group.

The two in the older group each have a background that has to be laid out, and the problems they face are more complicated. In season one, the younger group faces more of the difficulty of getting along and getting things done — obstacles you can clear one at a time.

With the older group we went into where their personalities came from, and the people around them get more to do as well. Some viewers ask why Dr. Zhao has so little screen time; that's because of Qu Xiaoxiao, who also has her reasons for becoming Qu Xiaoxiao. What people care about is whether she gets hold of the family money and where her family is heading. Whether Little Earthworm gets a foothold in Shanghai, and who she'll meet. Whether Guanguan becomes another Andy, or goes dark, as people put it. All of that will show up in season two.

It's about what each season emphasizes. Five parallel lines still need weighting.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702141643aiBGe791gN0kYbr5.jpg-w600)

**Q: If everyone has to be real and flawed, "why not show Old Tan with a young model on one arm and a starlet on the other?"**

Y: (Laughs) We didn't know Jin Dong was coming. This character was written flat, because he's a plot-thread character. Put simply, he connects to Andy and nobody else. He has no further overlap with the five girls and comes online only when Andy needs him, so we made no point of depicting his life.

The five girls are our center, and through them we reach into every part of society. Take Old Yan — nobody cares whether he has a wife either, right? (Laughs) Mostly it's that Jin Dong is too handsome, which complicates matters. We weren't trying to make the character perfect; we only took one slice of him.

**Q: "After reading the book I looked forward to Old Tan, and he ended up as the thin, label-like figure of the perfect domineering-CEO boyfriend from a Mary Sue romance." What's the function of Jin Dong's character? A lot of people love him, with almost no complaints — did you see that coming?**

Y: I answered part of that already. Also, he isn't a boyfriend, he's just a handsome face. I didn't expect the character to have this much presence either, because I didn't know Jin Dong would play him.

**Q: When Jin Dong and Wang Kai joined the production, were they famous yet?**

Y: Neither of them was. Sometimes you can't foresee these things. Their fans do mind that we didn't give them more material. Both are very good actors and we could have given them more scenes, but the characters were already set. We work from the characters. So even after they became famous, we didn't want to damage the characters for that. As the story develops, their personalities will come out when it's their turn.

**Q: Did they become famous partway through the shoot?**

Y: Yes. We started shooting in September. I remember it clearly: *The Disguiser* had just started airing when we began. A month or two in, *Nirvana in Fire* started airing too. And I remember clearly that director Kong watched it every night, and I'd tag along and watch.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702141643nCof0p72qcRXdBFK.jpg-w600)

**Q: A lot of people complain they can't get used to the voiceover — lines like "a rose with thorns." Was driving the plot with voiceover in the script from the start?**

Y: The voiceover wasn't in the original script. But with five leads, we worried viewers would have trouble keeping up with the plot, so after discussion we added it.

**Q: Some say this is a failed Chinese *Sex and the City*, full of wishful thinking about the middle class. What's your response?**

Y: First, what counts as middle class? This show should cover every layer of urban China.

We didn't cover the countryside, of course, but from the five girls' families of origin to the boyfriends they date to the workplaces they're in, we touched on small towns, small counties, cities, provincial capitals, Shanghai, even people coming back from abroad. We're not confined to the middle class at all — and since the middle class is most of the urban population, our proportions match.

As for what counts as wishful thinking, I have even less idea. I'd need to know what it refers to before I could answer. Does being real mean being identical to reality? If that were the standard, nobody would watch television drama. We obviously draw on life and then condense it.

As for these girls, some people say their personalities go to extremes. That's because each of them merges traits from hundreds and hundreds of real girls. There's a dramatic calculation behind it, but that doesn't make it untrue. I think the sheer scale of the discussion the show has set off proves the point.

**Q: Some people feel this is "*Tiny Times* finally making a television series." What's your response?**

Y: Lining up like things for comparison is far too easy — either it's four leads versus five, or it's the same subject.

Besides friendship, we also reflect a lot of social problems and social reality, and that's probably where our style parts ways with *Tiny Times*. *Tiny Times* leans toward friendship, takes an idol-drama approach, and is a kind of nostalgia for youth.

The things we look at are heavier: favoring sons over daughters, families of origin, sharing a flat, urban relationships, getting ahead at work. We go wider, and also deeper and heavier.

**Q: "Watching Wang Kai gave me secondhand embarrassment several times. My favorite was when he gave the CD to Guanguan and then turned around and made fun of Fan Shengmei."**

Y: First, that comes from the novel. Second, it isn't as terrible as people say. I'm surprised at how highly everyone rates their own moral cultivation — like Qidian and Andy talking about the neighbors at home. I think everyone has done a little gossiping. (Laughs) As long as a character in the show is real, she'll gossip too. It doesn't say much about personal quality.

I don't believe people sit around every day discussing philosophy, theology and music. I think everyone is being a bit too quick to make a moral case of it.

Dr. Zhao is quite lovable, in fact. He's the sort who doesn't follow convention and has a sense of fun. His value is exactly that he's an elite who doesn't play by the rules. Elites often tie themselves up in frameworks. Dr. Zhao is a genuine elite who also has an earthy side. He isn't quoting the classics every minute; otherwise his relationship with Qu Xiaoxiao would never have formed. The two of them have a taste for mischief, and people do have that side.

The keynote we set for this show is that there are no fake people in it. I'm sure everyone has talked about other people with a boyfriend or partner. It's an utterly ordinary scene from life. And in his case, doing it was to some degree an act of concern, not necessarily real mockery.

**Q: "It feels as if the characters are reduced to labels, with dialogue and plot cobbled together to fit them."**

Y: Such as? Raising doubts is easy; different people take away different impressions, and we have to think about what a broad audience wants. Some people tell us the show moves too fast, others that it drags. Part of that is our own doing, and part of it comes down to each person's perception.

**Q: "The actors deliver their lines like they're reciting from a book."**

Y: They're fine, actually. The performances are all good. Some actors' style may not match certain people's taste, or if you've read the novel and have a fixed image in your head, it may feel different — but that doesn't mean it's inaccurate, since the show does adjust the book.

**Q: "Why use the elevator-scare scene? Some people find it a bit awkward."**

Y: Not at all, most people liked it. That scene lets the five of them break the ice fast, and it's also the first time all five are together. After getting through a crisis together, it's easier to open up to one another. And that stretch shows each of the five girls' personalities very clearly.

**Q: A few questions about social reality: "Do you really think China's neighborhood police would come and deal with a noise complaint by the book?"**

Y: They would. In Shanghai they do come out. I've had police come out in both Shanghai and Beijing. But I can't spend an hour of screen time making you wait for them.

**Q: "Episode one is nothing but bugs. How could neighbors in a Shanghai housing complex possibly get that mixed up in each other's lives?"**

Y: It's explained inside the show. If you watched episode one carefully, the reason is there.

**Q: "People from Nantong aren't that country, and there's no train from Nantong to Shanghai."**

Y: Right, the script doesn't say Nantong. The crew later shot on location in Nantong, and that's probably why people settled on Nantong. In the script the place names all stand in for somewhere else.

**Q: "I can't understand Qu Xiaoxiao constantly mocking Fan Shengmei for wearing street-stall clothes — would someone written like Fan Shengmei still want to be her good friend? And the point is, what Fan wears isn't some Taobao bestseller. It's all brands! It's Vipshop! Is it really all right to trash a sponsor like that?"**

Y: First, she has a lot of clothes, and not all of them are from Vipshop. Second, Qu Xiaoxiao has her wrong. As for why Qu Xiaoxiao has her wrong and hates mistresses, people may understand that in season two.

**Q: Many people liked the earlier stretch and stopped liking it later. When you laid the story out this way, did you expect viewers to react like that?**

Y: We expected a reaction, not one this fierce. The first 20 episodes were also where we made changes; they're mostly the girls' daily lives, and apart from the scumbag Bai episode there's no big conflict.

The reason people feel a change later is that the season's two biggest events come online then. That's different from the book, which puts Andy's whole background on the table at the start.

The first 20 episodes move at a light pace, so much so that many people took this for a sitcom or an urban comedy. That's a misunderstanding; we've always been making a drama about real life. It's like meeting a person: they seem one way at first, and only after a while do you find the pain they'd rather not show.

The scale of the discussion may have to do with people standing in different places, and we welcome it. It genuinely makes us feel this show was worth making.

**Q: "Does the novel have bad values?"**

Y: People can read the novel and see whether there's a problem. If you have the time, it's more objective to read the whole thing carefully before discussing its values. It's hard for us to judge.

I do think the novel gave us a very good foundation, so where it's good, we try to do it justice. At reflecting reality the novel does a fine job.

**Q: Does the show follow the novel closely?**

Y: Yes. Season one's main plot is fairly close to the novel; there's little real adjustment.

What we mainly added was detail, and we adjusted its style and pitch: the book is colder and harder, and we made it warmer. Also, the book digs more deeply into individual emotional fate, while we lean more toward the friendship and interplay among the five girls.

**Q: Is that the standard for season one only, or for all three seasons?**

Y: That standard should hold for all three seasons.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702141643VoYQjA3rL8NTJHdU.jpg-w600)

**Q: "Andy and Qidian actually broke up. Strong protest!!!!!! I understand the logic of the novelist and the screenwriter, but I firmly oppose writing it this way."**

Y: I'm upset about it too, and I hated to let it happen. But let's put an ellipsis there. It touches on spoilers and some people wouldn't like that, so let's leave it.

**Q: "I really hope Qu and Dr. Zhao split up and she gets an ending with a bit of comeuppance in it."**

Y: (Laughs) Little Qu will have her own troubles. She and Dr. Zhao will break up and get back together; as for the final outcome, everyone will have to wait and see.

**Q: "Could the two young women's acting in the chocolate-eating scene have been any more overblown? Did you think that scene would be hard to perform?"**

Y: It wasn't hard. I think they got good notices for it. I liked that stretch — it fit the characters well.

**Q: "Character is drawn at the cost of plot." What's your response?**

Y: For instance — how do you know I sacrificed the plot?! There has to be some benchmark; otherwise how would you know?

**Q: "What's the plan behind the open ending? Does Bao Yifan turning up mean Andy has to be rescued by an outside force?"**

Y: That isn't the ending, actually. It's our easter egg for season two. It gives people some hints about where season two's story may go, though season two might not open in the order this easter egg suggests. So Andy's story will keep unfolding, and there's a reason Little Boss Bao appears. Keep watching and you'll find out.

**Q: Are you imitating American television storytelling? And if so, why does it look so different from American shows?**

Y: Because we're in China, of course it's very different. You could say we borrowed their story structure; the five parallel lines probably resemble American shows somewhat.

We want to drive the show through characters rather than purely through plot. We wanted to try that, but whatever happens, we're telling a Chinese story, so it won't feel like an American show.

The whole industry really is still behind American television — our scripts, the camerawork, the acting, and the fact that an actor here can't work on nothing but this one role. So maybe all we can do is our best.

**Q: When will the next two seasons air?**

Y: Season two is fairly settled: we shoot it this September and it airs around April or May next year. Season three we're working on. Either way, we're aiming for one season a year.

**Q: Will the relationships in season two be as tangled and messy as *Gossip Girl*?**

Y: They won't, and I think people can already see that. Ours is a fairly realist subject, and we won't add conflict for the sake of conflict. We did the same in season one: the male characters weren't all online until around episode ten. There was no big conflict at the opening either, and some people said it was a pleasant watch but that they didn't feel much had happened.

So in order to keep the characters real, we gave up manufacturing conflict entirely. If these girls' personalities lead to conflict, conflict happens. If they don't, we're not going to invent it to grab eyeballs.

So there won't be melodramatic love triangles or crossed-over relationships either. The five girls are so different in character that they could hardly fall for the same man. And you won't get that American-television thing where A is with B and then with C.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702141644Yf8IuFLiRJkXxUTd.jpg-w600)

**Q: What part did Hou Hongliang play in this show?**

Y: He's the producer, the boss. Our commander-in-chief. He took it seriously; he sat in on the bigger outlines we drew up and attended several of the discussion meetings.

And he was the key person. Now that the show has aired well enough and drawn plenty of response, doing a season two probably looks obvious. Back then it hadn't aired, and selling it may have been hard.

A women's drama with five parallel lines goes against ordinary viewing habits. At that point Mr. Hou insisted we do three seasons and build a contemporary-drama brand. That's where his foresight showed.

**Q: Do you go and read viewers' comments? How do they make you feel?**

Y: I do, often. Lately I see them everywhere I go, so I don't have to look. (How do they make you feel?) I should read less, or I won't know how to keep writing.

**Q: Would you say which character is your favorite?**

Y: Sure. Little Earthworm. She faces life with a kind of foolish courage; she's especially brave and warm. This world isn't afraid of you being slow, it's afraid of you going numb. I love the way Little Earthworm is. Her warmth and courage are unthinking, and they're the main force pushing society forward. In cities, seven or eight out of every ten people are like this, and she's the type I identify with most.

**Q: Your favorite scene?**

Y: There are quite a few; picking one is hard. I love the small ones, in fact. Like Little Earthworm's father coming to see her and cooking for her. Guanguan crying to Andy about being blamed by her boss, saying how hard it is to grow up. And I loved the scene where Andy is proposed to — that one was a joy to write. What else — after the trouble in the Fan family, Qu Xiaoxiao, Guanguan and Little Earthworm each tell their own family they love them. The scene where Qu Xiaoxiao makes that phone call especially; that one was a joy to write too.

**Q: Now that the show has finished airing, do you have regrets as its screenwriter?**

Y: Plenty. A television drama is a huge thing — 40-odd episodes may run to 500,000 words. There are certainly places that fall short: some of them not set up enough, the professional side not written with enough expertise, that sort of thing.

There are shortcomings, definitely. In season one we sometimes couldn't find the right locations, so we didn't get as close to the book as we wanted; some scenes we wrote were cut, or couldn't be shot, or didn't come out the way we'd imagined once they were.

At the end of the day this is teamwork, and all we can say is that we tried. The good thing is we have a chance to make up for it. There's still the next season.
